title: Make infrastructure changes reviewable
outcome: Use Terraform's configuration, plan, state and apply workflow deliberately.
introduction: Manual cloud commands created resources one at a time. Terraform records a desired configuration and asks providers to compare it with observed resources. You will first use a local file so every create, replacement and deletion is visible without cloud charges.

The same review discipline later applies to AWS. A plan describes proposed changes; apply executes them; state connects Terraform addresses to real objects. None of these files is a substitute for observing the actual service.
prerequisites: Weeks 13–16: distinguish identity, resource ownership, cost and cleanup. Use Ubuntu Bash and Git.
Work in ~/dev-opps-lab/infra/local17. This lesson's managed files stay in that directory. No cloud resources are created.

concepts.title: Configuration, provider, state and plan
paragraphs: Configuration describes intent. A provider implements operations for a particular API or local resource. State records which real object belongs to an address such as local_file.notice. A plan compares intent with state and refreshed observations.

Terraform can delete an object when its resource leaves configuration. State therefore matters: losing it does not delete infrastructure, but loses the normal ownership mapping. Store it privately and recoverably.
concepts.example: local_file.notice is an address in Terraform; notice.txt is the actual filesystem path it manages.
concepts.judgment: Read every create, update, replacement and deletion before apply. An unexpected resource or account is a reason to stop.

concepts.title: Immutability and sensitive data
paragraphs: Some changes are in-place updates; others require replacement. A provider decides which attributes require a new object. Replacing a local file is cheap, while replacing a database may affect data and downtime.

A sensitive label suppresses normal display; it does not magically remove a value from state or a saved plan. Keep these artifacts away from public Git and grant access only to operators who need them.
concepts.example: Changing a filename can remove the old managed file and create the new one. The plan must make that consequence explicit.
concepts.judgment: Commit configuration and dependency lock, but not state, plan files or credentials. Reproducibility means exact dependencies plus understood inputs, not publishing secrets.

steps.title: Install and record Terraform
steps.purpose: Run on the disposable Linux learning environment. These commands add HashiCorp's signed Ubuntu package source, then install its CLI.

commands.code:
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y gnupg wget lsb-release
wget -O- https://apt.releases.hashicorp.com/gpg | gpg --dearmor | sudo tee /usr/share/keyrings/hashicorp-archive-keyring.gpg > /dev/null
echo "deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/hashicorp-archive-keyring.gpg] https://apt.releases.hashicorp.com $(lsb_release -cs) main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/hashicorp.list
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y terraform
terraform version
explain: apt refreshes the package index and installs key/download tools. wget -O- writes the public signing key to stdout; gpg --dearmor converts it to the binary keyring; tee writes the system keyring with sudo.

lsb_release -cs selects the Ubuntu codename. signed-by limits this source's accepted signing key. The second apt update reads that source, install adds Terraform, and version records what was installed.
commands.troubleshoot: If package signature verification fails, stop and inspect the configured key/source rather than disabling verification. Do not rerun installation if Terraform is already appropriately installed.

steps.checkpoint: Save the installed version in your evidence.

steps.title: Define one resource
steps.purpose: A quoted heredoc preserves Terraform syntax and variable interpolation for Terraform, not Bash.

explain: mkdir creates the exact learning directories. The resource writes only into output; validation disallows directory separators in filenames. content is the managed text and 0644 means owner write, others read.

The provider constraint selects a compatible 2.x release; init downloads it and records the exact selected release/checksums in .terraform.lock.hcl. fmt normalizes formatting; validate checks configuration structure.
The local .gitignore excludes downloaded providers, state and saved plans without excluding the dependency lock.
commands.expected: init completes and validate reports configuration valid.
commands.troubleshoot: A provider download failure is an installation/network problem; inspect it before running apply. A syntax error needs its file/line fixed, not bypassed.

steps.checkpoint: Explain each HCL block before proceeding.

steps.title: Review and apply the saved plan
steps.purpose: A plan file binds the reviewed proposed actions to the later apply.

commands.code:
terraform plan -out=create.tfplan
terraform show -no-color create.tfplan
terraform apply create.tfplan
cat output/notice.txt
terraform state list
terraform plan -detailed-exitcode
printf "Plan exit status: %s\n" "$?"
explain: plan -out writes a binary plan; show renders it for review. Apply that exact file only after verifying one local_file creation and no unrelated actions.

cat observes the real output; state list shows Terraform's tracked address. -detailed-exitcode returns 0 for no changes, 2 for changes and 1 for an error. Capture $? immediately because any later command replaces it.
commands.expected: One file is created, state lists local_file.notice, and the final plan returns status 0.
commands.troubleshoot: A final status 2 means changes remain; read them rather than treating all nonzero statuses as errors. Status 1 requires diagnosis.

steps.checkpoint: Record the real file, tracked address and converged no-change plan.

steps.title: Preserve the right artifacts
steps.purpose: Review the Git change before committing; state never belongs in public history.

commands.code:
git status --short
git add main.tf .gitignore .terraform.lock.hcl
git diff --cached
git commit -m "Describe and verify a local Terraform resource"
explain: status reveals which files would enter version control. add names only configuration, ignore rules and dependency lock. diff --cached reviews exactly staged content; commit records it.
commands.expected: A commit with no tfstate, plan or credentials.
commands.troubleshoot: If this folder is not under the week-1 Git repository, return to ~/dev-opps-lab and verify its .git directory before initializing any new repository.

steps.checkpoint: In a note, translate the idea to aws_s3_bucket: a provider would call AWS instead of writing a file; identity and cost checks must precede apply.

failure.title: Predict a replacement before accepting it
failure.boundary: Only the managed local file inside infra/local17/output.

explain: The alternate input changes the managed path. This creates a plan only, not a filesystem change.
inject.expected: A replacement action is shown for local_file.notice.
inject.troubleshoot: If output differs with a future provider version, read the actual actions and record that behavior instead of assuming replacement.

investigate.code:
ls -l output
terraform state show local_file.notice
explain: ls observes existing files; state show reads the recorded resource attributes. Neither applies the plan.
investigate.expected: The current notice still exists before apply.
investigate.troubleshoot: If an earlier run changed it, first reconcile the current state and configuration before interpreting this comparison.

hints: Look for the old and new filename and the replacement marker.
An action in a saved plan has not happened yet.

explanation: Changing a resource's identity/location can require replacement. Accept this one because the lab file is disposable and contains no unique data; the same plan shape on a production database deserves much more scrutiny.

recover.code:
terraform apply replace.tfplan
terraform plan -out=restore.tfplan
terraform show -no-color restore.tfplan
terraform apply restore.tfplan
explain: Apply the reviewed replacement to observe it, then plan with the original default filename and review the reverse replacement before applying.
recover.expected: The managed file returns to output/notice.txt.
recover.troubleshoot: Do not manually delete state to undo a replacement; change desired configuration and review the recovery plan.

explain: test checks the actual expected file. A no-change plan checks convergence with the original input.
verification.expected: File exists and plan status is 0.
verification.troubleshoot: If status 2, read the remaining difference before marking the exercise complete.

questions.prompt: Why is state not a disposable cache?
questions.answer: It maps Terraform addresses to real resources and may contain important values. Removing it can orphan resources from normal management without deleting them.
It does not guarantee the value is absent from state or plans. Protect those artifacts separately.
It records the exact proposed actions and inputs. A fresh apply can generate different actions after configuration or observed state changes.

exercise.brief: Add a second clearly named local notice and prove its lifecycle.
constraints: No shell provisioners and no cloud provider yet.
deliverables: Reviewed create plan, both file contents, no-change plan and a scoped removal plan.
acceptance: The second file is independently addressed.
Removing its resource deletes only that file.
Configuration and lock are committed; state remains private.
hints: Use a second local_file resource with a different Terraform name and fixed filename.
solution: Define local_file.handoff, plan and apply it, then remove just that block and inspect the resulting single delete. This demonstrates desired-state removal rather than manual filesystem cleanup.

cleanup.code:
terraform plan -destroy -out=destroy.tfplan
terraform show -no-color destroy.tfplan
terraform apply destroy.tfplan
explain: Create and review a destroy plan for this root module; it should contain only the lab's local files. Applying deletes those managed files, not configuration or evidence.
cleanup.expected: Managed local resources are removed and no cloud charges exist.
cleanup.troubleshoot: If the plan contains any unfamiliar resource, stop: you are in the wrong Terraform directory or state.
